direction.premise: Several falling pieces occupy one shared stack rather than separate competitive wells.
direction.composition: A fitted vertical falling-block well sits between the small team score and two large rows of touch commands.
direction.shapeLanguage: Square bevelled blocks, block previews and chunky rectangular arcade buttons retain the source arcade silhouette.
direction.surfaceAndMaterial: Opaque pink and cyan bevels sit on the dark stack field; purple cabinet chrome remains outside the falling grid.
direction.paletteLogic: Each player owns a fixed vivid piece color, so active and locked cells remain attributable on the shared board.
direction.typography: The recovered arcade monospace labels distinguish score, piece actions and room state with short text.
direction.signature: Two colored active pieces share one authoritative well; a hard drop becomes the same locked cells on every connected screen.
direction.distinction: FOG uses geographic orders and ZAMAZKA uses painted restoration fragments; this port retains its source game object and the specific input loop described here.

architecture.primaryVerb: Move and rotate your own falling piece, then drop it into the shared stack while leaving room for the other player.
architecture.physicalFeedback: Touch movement changes a piece immediately in local play; online actions resolve into the same complete board snapshot for all peers.
architecture.spatialRationale: A fitted vertical falling-block well sits between the small team score and two large rows of touch commands. This keeps the current game object and its real inputs spatially connected on a phone.

comparisons.spatialDifference: CRUMPLE YARD uses a full-bleed 3D yard with a third-person car as its focus; Blockies uses one narrow framed vertical well, where every falling cell is a shared tactical constraint.
comparisons.interactionDifference: CRUMPLE YARD relies on continuous steering and physical deformation after impacts; Blockies uses discrete grid inputs, synchronized gravity and cooperative line clears across independent players.

comparisons.spatialDifference: TRACE MOSAIC uses an open workbench with a square picture grid and movable fragment tray; Blockies uses a tall falling-block well flanked only by ownership and next-piece indicators.
comparisons.interactionDifference: TRACE MOSAIC paints temporary drag-path barriers between other players; Blockies creates permanent shared stack geometry from locked pieces and rewards line clears.

production.renderer: Canvas 2D preserves the source block renderer and original collision, scoring and line-clear engine on the server.
production.focalAsset: The original bevelled block stack is the main rendered object; the authored interlocking-block SVG supplies the install identity.

motion.character: Grid movement snaps one cell at a time; the original gravity timer drops pieces discretely rather than interpolating their falling positions.
motion.action: Move and rotate your own falling piece, then drop it into the shared stack while leaving room for the other player.
motion.anticipation: The current selection, room state and available control labels expose the pending operation before the player activates it.
motion.response: The next visible state responds to the actual control: Two colored active pieces share one authoritative well; a hard drop becomes the same locked cells on every connected screen.
motion.followThrough: The resulting world, board or round state remains visible until a later explicit action changes it; no decorative transition hides the outcome.
motion.interruption: Repeated input uses the current state; pointer cancellation releases held controls and hidden tabs stop transmitting held actions.
motion.reducedMotion: The complete play state remains legible without decorative entry animations; spatial gameplay and authoritative outcomes retain their original timing.

evidence.expectedChange: The solo stack opens with one controllable falling piece, a next-piece preview and fitted touch controls.
